noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate the role of environmental factors in determining the rate of transpiration from a leafy shoot

primer.text: How do you measure something as invisible as evaporation from a leaf? Clamp the stem into a potometer, watch an air bubble crawl along a capillary tube, and let light, wind, humidity or warmth do their work. This practical note measures water loss honestly — including where the method cheats.

lessons.title: Potometers, the Measuring Devices
lessons.opening: Two potometer designs quantify water loss: a mass potometer weighs the water evaporating away, while a bubble potometer tracks the uptake of water that replaces it, with lamp, ruler, timer and shoot as the core kit.
keyPoints: A mass potometer records the plant's changing mass.
A bubble potometer records water uptake along a capillary tube.
Both estimate how fast a leafy shoot is losing water.
The kit includes a timer, a lamp, a ruler and the plant.
Environmental factors tested include light, wind, humidity and temperature.

low.restatement: Weigh the plant (mass potometer) or watch the bubble move (bubble potometer) to score transpiration.
low.analogy: Checking a fuel tank by weight or by watching the gauge — two gauges, one consumption story.
low.examPointer: Name both potometer types; questions often ask which is which.

medium.restatement: Uptake stands in for loss because the column of water is continuous: every molecule evaporated from the leaf drags a replacement up the stem.
medium.analogy: A conveyor belt: the parcel removed at the top is replaced at the bottom, so the belt's motion tracks the removal rate.
medium.examPointer: Justify using uptake as a proxy — the continuity of the water column is the accepted answer line.

check.stem: What does a bubble potometer measure directly?

options.text: The uptake of water by the shoot
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The mass lost by the plant
options.explanation: That is the mass potometer's reading.
Humidity is a factor tested, not the measurement.
Stomatal aperture is not recorded by any potometer.

check.stem: What does a mass potometer measure directly?

options.text: The change in mass of the plant as water evaporates
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That belongs to the bubble potometer.
The shoot sits in the potometer, out of soil.
Temperature is a tested factor, not the reading.

check.stem: Why can water uptake stand in for water loss?

options.text: The continuous water column means each evaporated molecule pulls a replacement up the stem
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Leaves do not hoard the incoming water.

options.text: Because the potometer adds water chemically
options.explanation: Nothing chemical replaces the loss.

options.text: Because uptake and loss are unrelated
options.explanation: They track each other through the water column.

check.stem: Which environmental factors can this practical test?

options.text: Light intensity, air movement, humidity and temperature
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Those affect growth, not this evaporation measurement.
Neither is an environmental factor in the set.
Wind is one of four factors, not the only one.

check.stem: Which piece of kit sets the light intensity in this investigation?

options.text: A lamp placed at measured distances from the shoot
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A fan varies air movement, not light.
The bag raises humidity.
It reads temperature; it does not set it.

check.stem: Name the two potometer types and what each records.
check.modelAnswer: A mass potometer records mass change; a bubble potometer records water uptake.

check.stem: List the apparatus for the light-intensity version of the practical.
check.modelAnswer: Potometer, timer, lamp, ruler and plant.

check.stem: Explain why the shoot is cut underwater before assembly.
check.modelAnswer: Cutting underwater stops air entering the xylem, since an air lock would break the continuous water column and stall the flow.

check.stem: A student wants to test wind speed instead of light. Name the factor they change and one control they must keep.
check.modelAnswer: They change the air movement, for example with a fan, while keeping temperature or humidity controlled.

lessons.title: Running the Light-Intensity Trial
sourceHeadings: Investigating the effect of light intensity on transpiration using a bubble potometer
lessons.opening: The shoot is sealed in airtight, its leaves dried, and a single air bubble reset between runs; a lamp at 10, 20 and 40 centimetres supplies the changing light while the bubble's travel over 30 minutes supplies the data.
keyPoints: Cut the shoot underwater and seal every joint with petroleum jelly.
Dry the leaves so surface water cannot distort the result.
Allow 5-10 minutes for the plant to adapt at each distance.
Record the bubble's start and end positions over 30 minutes.
Rate equals the distance moved divided by the time taken.

low.restatement: Set the lamp, wait, time 30 minutes, read the bubble, divide distance by time.
low.analogy: Timing a toy car along a ruler track — same start line, same stopwatch, three lamp settings.
low.examPointer: The division step is examinable: rate = distance moved / time period.

medium.restatement: Adaptation pauses let stomata settle at each new intensity, and repeats at each distance expose any anomalous run.
medium.analogy: Letting eyes adjust in a cinema before judging the screen brightness.
medium.examPointer: Mention the airtight seal and the underwater cut together; both protect the water column.

check.stem: Why are the leaves dried before readings begin?

options.text: Surface water would evaporate too and inflate the apparent transpiration
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Drying reduces mass; the point is fairness.
Drying does not close stomata.
Cleanliness is not the reason cited.

check.stem: How long does the plant adapt at each lamp distance?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Thirty minutes is the timing window for the bubble, not adaptation.
Days belong to the respiration flask run.
Skipping adaptation leaves stomata unadjusted.

check.stem: How is the bubble's distance converted into a rate?

options.text: Distance moved by the bubble divided by the 30-minute period
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Multiplication inverts the rate logic.
Unrelated quantities cannot subtract.
That is the inverse of the rate.

check.stem: How is the air bubble reset between runs?

options.text: By opening the reservoir tap to move the bubble back
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By cutting a new shoot each time
options.explanation: The same shoot is reused across distances.

options.text: By refilling the capillary with ink
options.explanation: No ink is involved.

options.text: By waiting for it to drift back
options.explanation: The tap, not patience, resets it.

check.stem: What seals the gaps in the assembled potometer?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Tape is not the named sealant.
Rubber bungs alone leak; jelly completes the seal.
Cotton wool insulates flasks; it does not seal potometers.

check.stem: State the three lamp distances used in the method.
check.modelAnswer: The lamp sits at 10 cm, then 20 cm, then 40 cm from the leaf.

check.stem: State the formula used to obtain the transpiration rate.
check.modelAnswer: Rate of transpiration equals the distance moved by the bubble divided by the time period of 30 minutes.

check.stem: Explain why repeats at each distance are taken before moving the lamp.
check.modelAnswer: Repeats reveal anomalies and let a mean be taken, so one odd run cannot masquerade as the effect of the new distance.

check.stem: A bubble travels 32 mm in 30 minutes. Compute the rate and give its units.
check.modelAnswer: 32 divided by 30 gives about 1.07 mm per minute.

lessons.title: Results, Limitations and Fixes
lessons.opening: Closer lamps pull bigger rates — 1.07, 0.80 and 0.40 mm per minute down the distance table — because bright light opens stomata; but the lamp also warms the shoot, which is the method's honest flaw.
keyPoints: Rate falls as lamp distance grows: 1.07, 0.80, 0.40 mm per minute.
Bright light opens more stomata, raising evaporation.
The lamp heats the shoot, mixing two variables.
Room humidity and air movement drift uncontrolled.
Leaks and xylem blockages are the practical's fixable faults.

low.restatement: Short distance, fast bubble, high rate — and the lamp's heat is the catch.
low.analogy: A heater next to a curtain: the light test accidentally tests the draught too.
low.examPointer: Quote the three rates if the table is given; patterns score, waffle does not.

medium.restatement: The two-variable problem means light's effect is entangled with temperature's, so conclusions claim association rather than clean causation.
medium.analogy: Two taps filling one bucket: you know the bucket filled, not which tap did it.
medium.examPointer: Name temperature as the confounder and propose distance from a cool light source or a heat filter as the fix.

check.stem: What pattern did the results table show between lamp distance and bubble travel?

options.text: Closer lamp, greater bubble movement, higher rate
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The 10 cm run moved 32 mm, the largest travel.
The three rows show a clear descending pattern.
The 40 cm row moved only 12 mm.

check.stem: Why does bright light raise the transpiration rate?

options.text: More stomata open, so more water vapour escapes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Light acts through the stomata, not by radiating the water away.
No thickening occurs during the run.
The bubble tracks uptake, not light pressure.

check.stem: Which flaw mixes two variables in this design?

options.text: The lamp warms the shoot, so temperature varies alongside light intensity
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The bubble is too small to see
options.explanation: The bubble is visible; that is not the cited flaw.
Measurement is fine; the confounding is the issue.
Shoots survive well enough for the 30-minute runs.

check.stem: How can an air-blocked xylem be avoided?

options.text: Cut the stem underwater and assemble the equipment underwater too
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Blow through the stem to clear it
options.explanation: Blowing adds what it claims to remove.
Thickness does not prevent air entry.
Light is irrelevant to the blockage.

check.stem: Which room factors drift during the experiment and threaten validity?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Neither varies meaningfully indoors.
Equipment economics is not an experimental factor.
Those are held constant by the CORMS design.

check.stem: State the three rates recorded in the results table.
check.modelAnswer: 1.07, 0.80 and 0.40 mm per minute at 10, 20 and 40 cm.

check.stem: Name two fixable faults listed in the limitations.
check.modelAnswer: Imperfect seals that leak, and blockages in the plant cutting.

check.stem: Explain why the result at 10 cm may overstate the pure light effect.
check.modelAnswer: Because the closest lamp also heats the shoot most, so part of the measured rise comes from temperature rather than from light intensity alone.

check.stem: Propose one improvement to isolate light from temperature in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: Place a heat filter or a water screen between lamp and shoot, or use a cool LED source, so light intensity changes while temperature stays level.

lessons.title: Further Factors and the CORMS Frame
lessons.opening: The same potometer tests the remaining factors — a fan for airflow, a misted bag for humidity, different rooms for temperature — and CORMS locks each variant into a fair design.
keyPoints: Airflow is set with a fan or hairdryer.
Humidity is raised by spraying a bag wrapped around the plant.
Temperature is varied by choosing cold or warm rooms.
CORMS: Change, Organisms, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
For light trials, the measurement is bubble distance in 30 minutes.

low.restatement: Fan for wind, bag for humidity, rooms for temperature; CORMS keeps every variant fair.
low.analogy: One adjustable dial per test: change it, hold the rest, read the gauge.
low.examPointer: Write the CORMS letters expanded; the acronym alone earns little.

medium.restatement: CORMS forces the changed factor to be the only systematic difference, with matched shoots, repeats and fixed measurement windows carrying the reliability.
medium.analogy: A fair-test contract signed before the experiment starts.
medium.examPointer: Match each letter to this practical's own details, not to a generic answer.

check.stem: How is humidity increased in the further experiments?

options.text: Spray water into a plastic bag and wrap it around the plant
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: By pointing a fan at the shoot
options.explanation: A fan changes air movement, not humidity.

options.text: By moving the plant to a cold room
options.explanation: Rooms change temperature.
Drying lowers local humidity, if anything.

check.stem: In the CORMS frame for the light trial, what is the Organisms requirement?

options.text: The same species, size, age and number of leaves in every repeat
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Any plant available at the time
options.explanation: Unmatched shoots break the fair test.
The same shoot is reused.
Removing leaves changes the organism itself.

check.stem: What is measured in the CORMS Measurement slot for the light trial?

options.text: The distance the bubble travels, in 30 minutes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The lamp supplies the change, not the reading.
Temperature belongs to the Same list.
Height is irrelevant to this measurement.

check.stem: Which factor is investigated with a hairdryer?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A hairdryer moves air; misted bags raise humidity.
The lamp investigates light.
Soil temperature is not this shoot's tested factor.

check.stem: Why must temperature, wind and humidity sit in the Same list for the light trial?

options.text: So the changed factor is the only systematic difference between runs
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because they are impossible to measure
options.explanation: They are measurable; they must merely stay fixed.

options.text: Because they have no effect on transpiration
options.explanation: They affect it strongly, which is exactly why they must be held.

options.text: Because the CORMS letters must all be used
options.explanation: Letters earn their place by role, not by quota.

check.stem: State how temperature is varied in the further experiments.
check.modelAnswer: By running the practical in a cold room or a warm room.

check.stem: Expand the CORMS acronym.
Explain why the plastic-bag method tests humidity without starving the shoot.
check.modelAnswer: The bag encloses the air around the leaves, raising its humidity, while the stem still draws water from the potometer reservoir, so the shoot stays supplied.

check.stem: Draft a CORMS plan for the humidity variant.
check.modelAnswer: Change the bag's internal humidity; keep the same shoot species, size and leaves; repeat each condition; measure bubble distance in 30 minutes; hold temperature, light and airflow the same.

glossary.definition: Apparatus that measures water uptake or mass loss to estimate transpiration.
The tracked marker in a bubble potometer's capillary tube.
Leaf pores whose opening responds to light and governs water-vapour loss.
The design prompt: Change, Organisms, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
